name_en: Schedule one pleasant or meaningful activity
name_ar: جدولة نشاط ممتع أو ذي معنى
what: Each day, deliberately put one enjoyable or values-linked activity (e.g., sketching, a call with a friend, a café with a book, volunteering) into the calendar as a real block, then do it and rate enjoyment/meaning 0–10. Behavioral-activation style: plan the activity rather than waiting to feel like it.
why: Behavioral activation (scheduling valued, enjoyable activities) improved well-being vs controls (Hedges g = 0.52) including in non-clinical participants.

sources.title: Behavioral activation interventions for well-being: A meta-analysis
Meta-analyses of positive psychology interventions: The effects are much smaller than previously reported

cue_suggestion: While doing the evening plan for tomorrow (after Isha)
minimum_version: 5 minutes of something you enjoy, logged
joy_pairing: Keep a personal 'joy menu' list and pick from it; alternate solo and social items for novelty
friction_down: App offers 3 picks from her own joy menu; pre-book time block
friction_up_for_competing: Phone on focus mode during the block
if_then_plan: If my evening plan has no enjoyable block for tomorrow, then I will pick one item from my joy menu and give it a time.
safety_or_stop_rule: Non-clinical wellbeing use only. If low mood persists for about two weeks or daily functioning drops, see JOY-13 and contact a professional.
notes: Mazzucchelli pooled effect is from 20 small RCTs; White 2019 shows positive-psychology-type effects shrink when small-sample bias is corrected, so expect modest benefits.

what: Once a day, slow down during a pleasant moment (tea, sunset, a finished task, a laugh with family) for a minute: notice sensations, say what is good about it, and optionally share it or note it.
why: A 2026 meta-analysis of 20 RCTs (n=4,805) found savoring interventions had a moderate pooled effect on emotional outcomes (g = 0.51).

sources.title: Effectiveness of savoring interventions: A systematic review and meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials

minimum_version: 3 slow breaths noticing one good thing
normal_version: 1–3 minutes of deliberate savoring + one-line note
bonus_version: Share the moment with someone or photograph it for the weekly review
joy_pairing: Attach to a treat she already enjoys (favorite drink, sunset walk)
friction_down: One-tap note field with photo option
friction_up_for_competing: Don't open social media during the first sip
if_then_plan: If I sit down with my afternoon drink, then I will spend one minute noticing what is good right now.
safety_or_stop_rule: None specific; non-clinical wellbeing practice.
notes: Effect larger vs passive than active controls (not significant moderator); newest MA, treat size cautiously.

what: A few times a week, write 1–3 specific things you are grateful for, or occasionally express thanks to a person (message/letter). Mixing gratitude activity types is fine.
why: A 2025 cross-cultural meta-analysis (145 papers, 28 countries) found gratitude interventions produce small increases in well-being (g = 0.19); effects were larger when multiple gratitude activity types were combined.

sources.title: A meta-analysis of the effectiveness of gratitude interventions on well-being across cultures
Using Gratitude to Promote Positive Change: A Series of Meta-Analyses Investigating the Effectiveness of Gratitude Interventions

cue_suggestion: Before sleep, after closing the day's plan
bonus_version: Send a thank-you message to someone
joy_pairing: Use a pretty notebook or a brand-styled card template in the app; vary format (list, letter, photo)
friction_down: Prompt appears inside the evening shutdown
if_then_plan: If I finish my evening review, then I will write one thing I'm grateful for today.
safety_or_stop_rule: If it starts to feel forced or guilt-inducing, reduce frequency or switch type; it is optional.
notes: Effects are SMALL; Dickens 2017 concluded benefits may be overemphasized. Keep light, don't oversell in the app.

what: Plan and do small deliberate acts of kindness for family, friends, colleagues or strangers (help, a gift, a kind message); log them.
why: A meta-analysis of 27 studies (N=4,045) found performing kindness has a small-to-medium effect on the actor's well-being (δ = 0.28).

sources.title: Happy to help? A systematic review and meta-analysis of the effects of performing acts of kindness on the well-being of the actor

cue_suggestion: Sunday planning (choose the day); do on that day
normal_version: One planned act of kindness on a chosen day
joy_pairing: Do it with a sibling/friend; pick acts that match her skills (e.g., help someone's CV/portfolio)
if_then_plan: If it's my chosen kindness day, then I will do one act from my list before Maghrib.
safety_or_stop_rule: Keep within her time/energy and budget; kindness should not become obligation or overcommitment.
notes: Dose/frequency not specified by source.

name_en: Keep in touch with people who matter
what: Maintain regular contact with close friends/family: a call, visit, shared activity, or being fully present (phone away) during conversations; optionally join a group or volunteer.
why: Across 148 studies, stronger social relationships were associated with a 50% increased likelihood of survival (OR 1.50); WHO highlights everyday steps such as reaching out to a friend, putting the phone away in conversation, joining a group or volunteering.

sources.title: Social relationships and mortality risk: a meta-analytic review
WHO news release: Social connection linked to improved health and reduced risk of early death (WHO Commission on Social Connection report)

cue_suggestion: Thursday evening / weekend; or a fixed 'call day'
normal_version: One call/visit with a close person this week
bonus_version: Join a community/UX group meetup or volunteer
joy_pairing: Combine with walks, coffee, co-working or cooking together
friction_down: App keeps a short 'people I want to stay close to' list with last-contact date
if_then_plan: If someone on my list hasn't heard from me in two weeks, then I will send them a message that day.
safety_or_stop_rule: Feeling persistently lonely or isolated is a reason to reach out for support (JOY-13).
notes: Holt-Lunstad is observational (association). No source specified a contact frequency; the two-week trigger is a user-adjustable app default, not an evidence dose.

what: Spend recreational time in natural settings (parks, corniche/seafront, gardens, desert outings), in one visit or several shorter ones.
dose: ≥120 min/week of recreational nature contact was associated with better self-reported health and well-being; associations peaked at 200–300 min/week; it did not matter whether reached in one long or several short visits (observational).
why: Nature contact ≥120 min/week was associated with higher odds of good health and high well-being; greenspace exposure is associated with lower cortisol and heart rate among other outcomes.

sources.title: Spending at least 120 minutes a week in nature is associated with good health and wellbeing
The health benefits of the great outdoors: A systematic review and meta-analysis of greenspace exposure and health outcomes

cue_suggestion: Pair with the evening walk after Maghrib or a weekend outing
minimum_version: 10 minutes outside near greenery or the sea
normal_version: Several walks/visits totalling ~120 min across the week
bonus_version: A weekend half-day outing (park, beach, mountain area)
joy_pairing: Go with family/friends, bring a favorite drink, photograph textures for her design moodboard
friction_down: Save 3 nearby green/sea spots in the app
if_then_plan: If the weekend arrives and my nature minutes are under target, then I will plan one outing for Friday or Saturday evening.
safety_or_stop_rule: Avoid peak heat hours in Makkah/Jeddah; carry water; go at safe times/places, ideally accompanied.
notes: White 2019 is cross-sectional (UK); can overlap with walking actions from the BODY cluster.

what: Protect regular time for a non-work creative or leisure activity she enjoys (drawing, lettering, photography, crafts, music, cooking) — distinct from portfolio work.
why: In young adults, days with more creative activity than usual were followed by higher positive affect and flourishing; more enjoyable leisure activities were associated with better psychosocial and physical measures.

sources.title: Everyday creative activity as a path to flourishing
Association of enjoyable leisure activities with psychological and physical well-being

cue_suggestion: A fixed weekend slot or one weekday evening
joy_pairing: Choose purely for fun; no output pressure; background music
friction_up_for_competing: Log out of short-video apps during the slot
if_then_plan: If it's my hobby evening, then I will set out materials right after dinner.
safety_or_stop_rule: Keep it separate from performance goals; if it becomes another KPI, remove tracking.
notes: Evidence is observational (daily diary, cross-sectional). The 16-country hobby study (Mak 2023) was excluded: 65+ population.

what: When she misses a plan, makes a mistake or feels self-critical: acknowledge the difficulty, remember everyone struggles, and speak to herself as she would to a friend, then choose the next small step.
why: A meta-analysis of 27 RCTs found self-compassion interventions improved outcomes including rumination, stress, depression, self-criticism and anxiety vs controls.

sources.title: Self-Compassion Interventions and Psychosocial Outcomes: a Meta-Analysis of RCTs

cue_suggestion: Triggered by a missed task or harsh self-talk
normal_version: 2–5 minute written or spoken self-compassion break
friction_down: App shows the prompt automatically after a skipped habit, in neutral language
if_then_plan: If I notice I'm calling myself lazy or a failure, then I will write one kind sentence and pick the minimum version of the next task.
safety_or_stop_rule: Not a treatment. If self-criticism is severe or persistent, see JOY-13.
notes: Pairs with engine rule on lapses (ENG-19). Populations and intervention types in the MA were diverse; publication bias possible.

what: Once a week, review what was planned vs done (physically recorded), note wins and joys, compare planned vs actual time, and plan next week using those real times.
why: Progress monitoring promoted goal attainment (d = 0.40), more so when progress was physically recorded or reported; linking predictions to past experience removed the optimistic bias in completion-time estimates.

sources.title: Does monitoring goal progress promote goal attainment? A meta-analysis of the experimental evidence
Exploring the "planning fallacy": Why people underestimate their task completion times

cue_suggestion: Same slot each week (e.g., Saturday morning or Thursday evening)
minimum_version: 5 min: 1 win, 1 lesson, top 3 for next week
joy_pairing: Favorite café, special drink, review the week's savored photos and gratitude notes
friction_down: App pre-fills the week's data and past time estimates
if_then_plan: If it's Saturday after breakfast, then I will open the weekly review.
safety_or_stop_rule: Review is informational, not a judgment; avoid red 'failure' framing.

what: Use natural temporal landmarks (start of week/month, new semester, birthday, after Ramadan/Eid) to launch or relaunch goals, with a short reset ritual.
why: Searches for dieting, gym visits and goal commitments increase after temporal landmarks, which people treat as new mental accounting periods ('fresh start effect').

sources.title: The Fresh Start Effect: Temporal Landmarks Motivate Aspirational Behavior

normal_version: Monthly 15-min reset: choose focus, re-set minimum versions
joy_pairing: Small celebration ritual (new playlist, clean desk, new wallpaper from her brand kit)
friction_down: App auto-suggests the next landmark after a lapse
if_then_plan: If I've fallen off a routine, then I will restart it on the next landmark (next Sunday or the 1st) with its minimum version.
safety_or_stop_rule: Don't wait for a landmark if restarting today is possible; landmarks are an extra boost, not a gate.
notes: Archival field data (associational); the effect on actual long-term success was not established by this source.

what: Schedule genuine rest: short micro-breaks between work blocks and daily off-time where she mentally detaches from work/study (no checking tasks). Rest counts as a completed plan item.
why: Micro-breaks had small significant effects on vigor (d = .36) and fatigue (d = .35); detachment from work during off-time correlates with less exhaustion, better sleep and well-being.

sources.title: "Give me a break!" A systematic review and meta-analysis on the efficacy of micro-breaks for increasing well-being and performance
A Meta-Analysis on Antecedents and Outcomes of Detachment from Work

cue_suggestion: End of each focus block; a fixed daily shutdown time
normal_version: Micro-breaks between blocks + an evening off-time with no work
bonus_version: One full work-free half-day per week
joy_pairing: Tea, stretching, stepping outside, chatting with family
friction_down: App schedules breaks automatically and shows them as 'done' items
if_then_plan: If I finish a focus block, then I will stand up and take a short break before the next one.
safety_or_stop_rule: n/a
notes: Detachment MA is correlational and in employees; for highly depleting tasks micro-breaks under 10 min may be insufficient for performance.

what: If she chooses, the app lets her enter her own spiritual practices (e.g., prayer times as day anchors, reflection time). The app does not prescribe, rate, or gamify them.
why: Included only as a user-defined stable daily anchor for other habits; no wellbeing claim is made.
friction_down: Optional prayer-time integration as cues for other routines
tracking_metric: None by default (user may opt in)
safety_or_stop_rule: Never score, streak, or send guilt notifications about spiritual practice.
notes: Deliberately not evidence-dosed; per brief, not prescribed. Using fixed daily events as cues follows the habit context-stability rule (ENG-01).

name_en: Know when to seek help (Saudi lines)
what: Keep a visible help card: if low mood, anxiety, hopelessness or stress persist or interfere with daily life, contact a professional. Saudi MOH options: Psychological Consultation Center 920033360 (trained mental-health professionals; 8am–8pm daily, Saturdays 1–8pm per MOH page), 937 (24/7 medical consultations by phone), Qareboon app (supervised text counseling), primary care centers, and emergency departments (24h) for urgent situations.
why: MOH lists these as official psychological/medical consultation routes available across the Kingdom.

sources.title: Saudi MOH – Psychiatry / mental health services (Psychological Consultation Center 920033360, 937, Qareboon app, ER 24h)
Saudi MOH – 937 Service (24/7 medical consultation)

cue_suggestion: Pinned in app settings; surfaced if she logs very low mood repeatedly
if_then_plan: If I feel unable to cope or have thoughts of harming myself, then I will go to the nearest emergency department or call for urgent help immediately.
safety_or_stop_rule: Any thoughts of self-harm or danger = emergency department now (24h). The app must not attempt diagnosis or treatment.
notes: Hours for 920033360 were stated on the MOH page at fetch time (2026-09-28); re-verify periodically. The MOH 937 page itself does not specifically mention mental health; the psychiatry page lists 937 as medical consultation by voice call.

name_en: Anchor every habit to a stable cue
what: Each habit must have one stable context cue (same time/place or after an existing routine event, e.g., after Fajr, after breakfast) and be repeated in that context. The app asks for the cue when a habit is created and schedules it relative to that event.
why: Habits form as the same response is repeated in a recurring context (Wood & Rünger); a cue inside an existing daily routine is recommended as a stable starting point (Gardner 2012); context stability, morning timing, enjoyment and personal choice were among determinants of habit formation (Singh 2024).

sources.title: Psychology of Habit
Making health habitual: the psychology of 'habit-formation' and general practice
Time to Form a Habit: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis of Health Behaviour Habit Formation and Its Determinants

safety_or_stop_rule: If a cue keeps failing (e.g., schedule changed), prompt her to re-anchor rather than add reminders.

what: Never promise '21 days'. Show that automaticity typically takes around two months or more and varies widely; simple actions become automatic faster. Start with small, simple versions.
why: In Lally et al. automaticity plateaued on average ~66 days after first daily performance, with wide variation, and simple actions peaked faster (as summarized by Gardner 2012); a 2024 meta-analysis (20 studies, n=2,601) found median 59–66 days, means 106–154 days, individual range 4–335 days.

sources.title: How are habits formed: Modelling habit formation in the real world
Making health habitual: the psychology of 'habit-formation' and general practice
Time to Form a Habit: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis of Health Behaviour Habit Formation and Its Determinants

safety_or_stop_rule: If automaticity is not rising after many weeks, simplify the behavior or change the cue rather than blaming her.

name_en: A missed day is not a reset
what: Missing a single day must not reset progress or trigger failure messaging. The next scheduled occurrence shows the minimum version and a small 'welcome back' reward.
why: Automaticity gains soon resumed after one missed performance (Lally, summarized in Gardner 2012); in a 61,293-person megastudy, the top intervention offered micro-rewards for returning to the gym after a missed workout (Milkman 2021).

sources.title: Making health habitual: the psychology of 'habit-formation' and general practice
How are habits formed: Modelling habit formation in the real world
Megastudies improve the impact of applied behavioural science

safety_or_stop_rule: Repeated consecutive misses (e.g., a full week) trigger a gentle re-plan/fresh-start flow (ENG-19), not guilt.
notes: Evidence strength: Lally is an observational field study; Milkman is a large RCT (megastudy) in a gym-member population.

what: Every 2–4 weeks for each core habit, ask the 4 SRBAI items ('Behavior X is something I do automatically / without having to consciously remember / without thinking / before I realize I'm doing it') on an agreement scale; chart the trend. Graduate a habit to 'maintenance' when scores plateau high.
why: The Self-Report Behavioural Automaticity Index is a reliable 4-item automaticity subscale of the SRHI, suited to tracking habit formation (Gardner 2012 IJBNPA); Gardner 2012 BJGP suggests weekly self-ratings of how automatic a behavior feels.

sources.title: Towards parsimony in habit measurement: testing the convergent and predictive validity of an automaticity subscale of the Self-Report Habit Index
Making health habitual: the psychology of 'habit-formation' and general practice

safety_or_stop_rule: Keep it quick (under 1 minute); skip if she dismisses it twice in a row.
notes: Measurement frequency (2–4 weeks) is an app design choice, not a source dose. The validation work included a systematic review of SRHI applications plus primary datasets.

what: When she creates a task/habit, the app converts it into an if-then plan (If [time/place/cue], then I will [specific action]) and asks her to read it back once (rehearsal). Prefer her own wording.
why: Implementation intentions had a medium-to-large effect on goal attainment (d = .65, 94 tests; Gollwitzer & Sheeran 2006); across 642 tests effects ranged d = .27–.66 and were larger with a contingent if-then format, high goal motivation and rehearsal (Sheeran et al. 2024).

sources.title: Implementation Intentions and Goal Achievement: A Meta-analysis of Effects and Processes
The when and how of planning: Meta-analysis of the scope and components of implementation intentions in 642 tests

safety_or_stop_rule: If motivation for the goal is low, if-then plans help less; revisit whether the goal is still wanted (ENG-20).

what: For each core habit, the app asks: 'What is most likely to stop you?' and 'If that happens, then I will…' (obstacle-focused if-then). Optionally uses mental contrasting: wish → best outcome → main inner obstacle → if-then plan.
why: Mental contrasting with implementation intentions (MCII) improved goal attainment with a small-to-moderate effect (g = 0.336, 21 studies), stronger when interactive; publication bias suggests true effects may be smaller (Wang 2021). Sheeran 2024 taxonomy covers obstacle cues and responses in if-then plans.

sources.title: A Meta-Analysis of the Effects of Mental Contrasting With Implementation Intentions on Goal Attainment
The when and how of planning: Meta-analysis of the scope and components of implementation intentions in 642 tests

safety_or_stop_rule: Limit to 1–2 obstacles per habit to avoid planning overload.
notes: The task brief mentioned a '2024 Wang et al.' implementation-intentions MA; I could only verify Wang, Wang & Gai 2021 (MCII) and Sheeran et al. 2024 (642 tests). Sniehotta 2005 coping-planning paper was dropped (cardiac-rehab population).

what: When offering options for a habit (which workout, which study format), rank the most enjoyable acceptable option first, and ask her to rate enjoyment after sessions; use those ratings to recommend future versions.
why: Immediate rewards (e.g., enjoyment) predicted persistence in long-term goals more than delayed rewards (Woolley & Fishbach 2017); choosing the most enjoyable rather than most useful exercise, or adding immediate rewards like music, increased persistence (Woolley & Fishbach 2016).

sources.title: For the Fun of It: Harnessing Immediate Rewards to Increase Persistence in Long-Term Goals
Immediate Rewards Predict Adherence to Long-Term Goals

safety_or_stop_rule: Enjoyable option must still meet safety and minimum-effectiveness criteria from the relevant action (e.g., BODY cluster).

what: Let her pair a 'want' (favorite podcast, series-style audiobook, special drink) with a 'should' (walk, workout, chores), optionally restricting the want to that activity. Refresh bundles when enjoyment fades.
why: Gym-only access to tempting audiobooks initially increased gym visits by 51% (29% with encouragement only), but effects declined over time (Milkman 2014); in a 6,792-person field experiment, audiobooks plus encouragement to bundle raised weekly workout likelihood by 10–14% (Kirgios 2020); the Milkman 2021 megastudy tested many such digital nudges.

sources.title: Holding the Hunger Games Hostage at the Gym: An Evaluation of Temptation Bundling
Teaching temptation bundling to boost exercise: A field experiment

safety_or_stop_rule: Content paired with walking outdoors must not reduce traffic awareness (one earbud/low volume).
notes: Decay over time → the app should rotate bundles.

name_en: Don't pay her for what she already enjoys
name_ar: لا مكافآت مادية لما تحبه أصلاً
what: Avoid expected, tangible, task-contingent rewards (points-for-doing, badges-as-payment) for activities she already finds enjoyable (hobbies, creative work, reading for fun). Prefer informational positive feedback ('You walked 3 times — that's your plan working'). Reserve extrinsic rewards for dull tasks or getting started/returning.
why: Engagement-, completion- and performance-contingent tangible rewards undermined free-choice intrinsic motivation (d = −0.40, −0.36, −0.28), while positive feedback enhanced free-choice behavior (d = 0.33) and interest (d = 0.31) (Deci, Koestner & Ryan 1999; 128 studies).

sources.title: A meta-analytic review of experiments examining the effects of extrinsic rewards on intrinsic motivation

safety_or_stop_rule: If she reports an activity feels like 'a chore for points', remove tracking/rewards from it.

what: Every core goal has a one-tap log and a simple progress view; weekly review (JOY-09) reads it back. Offer optional sharing with a chosen accountability person.
why: Progress-monitoring interventions promoted goal attainment (d = 0.40, 138 studies) with larger effects when progress was physically recorded or reported/made public (Harkin 2016).

sources.title: Does monitoring goal progress promote goal attainment? A meta-analysis of the experimental evidence

safety_or_stop_rule: Sharing is opt-in only; no public leaderboards by default. Avoid monitoring that increases anxiety (e.g., constant weight tracking) — let her hide metrics.

name_en: Specific, challenging goals + visible closeness to goal
name_ar: أهداف محددة وتحفيز الاقتراب من الهدف
what: Goals must be specific and appropriately challenging, with a concrete weekly target; show progress as distance-to-goal (e.g., '2 of 3 sessions done — 1 to go') so the goal-gradient boost kicks in near the end. Break big outcome goals (pass IELTS band X, get driving licence) into process goals (sessions, practice tests) she controls.
why: Goal setting had a small positive unique effect on behavior (d = .34), strongest when goals were difficult, set publicly, or group goals (Epton 2017); people accelerate effort as they approach a reward and illusory progress (pre-filled stamps) sped completion (Kivetz 2006).

sources.title: Unique effects of setting goals on behavior change: Systematic review and meta-analysis
The Goal-Gradient Hypothesis Resurrected: Purchase Acceleration, Illusionary Goal Progress, and Customer Retention

safety_or_stop_rule: Difficult must stay achievable; if completion falls below ~half for several weeks, auto-suggest lowering the target.
notes: Process-vs-outcome goal split is a design choice; I did not find/verify a meta-analysis comparing them directly (gap). The ~half threshold is an app heuristic, not a source dose.

name_en: Light gamification; expect small, fading effects
what: Use game elements sparingly (progress bars, levels, gentle challenges) as support, not the engine; rotate/novelty-refresh them; never rely on them for long-term adherence.
why: Gamified interventions had a small-to-medium effect on physical activity (g = 0.42) that fell to very small-to-small at ~14-week follow-up (g = 0.15) (Mazeas 2022); vs non-gamified apps, gamification produced only trivial step increases (~489 steps/day) (Nishi 2024).

sources.title: Evaluating the Effectiveness of Gamification on Physical Activity: Systematic Review and Meta-analysis of Randomized Controlled Trials
Effect of digital health applications with or without gamification on physical activity and cardiometabolic risk factors: a systematic review and meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials

safety_or_stop_rule: Remove or simplify game elements she finds pressuring or childish.

what: If streaks are shown: define them flexibly (e.g., weekly targets like '3 of 7 days' instead of daily), include pre-set 'rest days'/repairs, never send 'you broke your streak' notifications, and attribute breaks to external factors where true.
why: Highlighting intact streaks increases subsequent engagement relative to highlighting broken streaks; the harm is amplified when people blame themselves and attenuated when they can repair a streak (Silverman & Barasch 2022, 7 studies).

sources.title: On or Off Track: How (Broken) Streaks Affect Consumer Decisions

safety_or_stop_rule: If she reports streak anxiety, hide streaks entirely.

name_en: Loss framing only as opt-in commitment
what: Loss-framed commitments (e.g., 'start the week with 5 points; lose one per missed session') are offered only if she opts in, for a specific goal and time window; default framing is positive.
why: In a 13-week RCT, a loss-framed incentive increased days meeting a 7,000-step goal vs control (0.45 vs 0.30), while equivalent gain and lottery incentives did not significantly differ from control (Patel 2016).

sources.title: Framing Financial Incentives to Increase Physical Activity Among Overweight and Obese Adults: A Randomized, Controlled Trial

safety_or_stop_rule: Stop loss framing if it causes stress; never use money penalties or guilt; the app should not use loss framing on rest, spiritual practice or mood.
notes: Population: overweight/obese employees with real money incentives; applying it to points is an extrapolation. priority: Optional.

name_en: Personal, tailored reminders with adaptive frequency
what: Reminders are personalized (her words, her cue), tailored to context, and their frequency decreases or adapts over time instead of staying fixed; each habit gets at most one reminder, tied to its cue.
why: Text-messaging interventions had an overall effect d = .329; tailoring/personalization and individualized or decreasing message frequency were associated with greater efficacy (Head 2013, 19 RCTs); most studies of periodic prompts reported positive findings (11/19) (Fry & Neff 2009).

sources.title: Efficacy of text messaging-based interventions for health promotion: a meta-analysis
Periodic prompts and reminders in health promotion and health behavior interventions: systematic review

safety_or_stop_rule: If she dismisses a reminder repeatedly, stop it and ask to re-anchor the cue (ENG-01).
notes: Fry & Neff: long-term effects were not examinable.

what: Send suggestions only at user-selected decision points and when context fits (e.g., free calendar slot, not driving, suitable weather/time); cap daily prompts; vary content; measure whether a prompt actually leads to the behavior in the next ~30 min and drop prompts that don't.
why: JITAIs aim to deliver the right type/amount of support at the right time by adapting to changing state (Nahum-Shani 2018). In the HeartSteps micro-randomized trial, walking suggestions increased 30-min step count (24% average), but the effect was largest at the start and decreased over time (Klasnja 2019).

sources.title: Just-in-Time Adaptive Interventions (JITAIs) in Mobile Health: Key Components and Design Principles for Ongoing Health Behavior Support
Efficacy of Contextually Tailored Suggestions for Physical Activity: A Micro-randomized Optimization Trial of HeartSteps

safety_or_stop_rule: Hard cap on daily notifications (her setting); silence during prayer/sleep/driving/study blocks.
notes: HeartSteps n=44 adults, 6 weeks — small trial; 'notification fatigue' is inferred from diminishing effects, not directly measured. Cap value is her choice (not source-specified).

what: Show at most a small set of options (e.g., 3) for 'what to do now'; keep a limited number of active goals per season (e.g., driving, IELTS, portfolio, fitness) and park others in a 'later' list.
why: Choice overload is more likely with complex choice sets, difficult decision tasks, preference uncertainty, and an effort-minimizing goal (Chernev 2015, 99 observations, N=7,202).

sources.title: Choice overload: A conceptual review and meta-analysis

safety_or_stop_rule: Let her override; limits are defaults, not locks.
notes: Specific numbers (3 options; 4 goals) are design defaults — no source specifies an optimal count of active goals (gap).

name_en: Buffer time using her own history
what: Estimate task durations from her actual past completion times (logged); add buffer blocks each day; never schedule 100% of free time.
why: People underestimate their own completion times by focusing on plan-based scenarios; the optimistic bias was eliminated when participants connected relevant past experiences to their predictions (Buehler 1994).

sources.title: Exploring the "planning fallacy": Why people underestimate their task completion times

safety_or_stop_rule: If more than half of planned blocks overrun in a week, reduce next week's load automatically (app heuristic).
notes: Buffer size is not specified by source.

what: Every habit has a minimum version. Each morning she can mark energy/mood (low/normal/high); low → app swaps in minimum versions and drops optional items; allow flexible time windows rather than rigid single slots for demanding habits like exercise.
why: Paying for gym visits within a fixed daily two-hour window produced fewer visits during and after the intervention than flexible incentives paid for visiting any time that day (Beshears 2021); small, manageable changes are recommended because failure is discouraging (Gardner 2012).

sources.title: Creating Exercise Habits Using Incentives: The Trade-off Between Flexibility and Routinization
Making health habitual: the psychology of 'habit-formation' and general practice

safety_or_stop_rule: Low-energy days that persist for weeks → suggest checking sleep/health and JOY-13 if mood-related.
notes: Tension with ENG-01 (stable cues): keep a stable cue but allow a window around it.

name_en: Treat lapses as lapses, not collapse
what: Language and flows distinguish a lapse (a slip) from a relapse (return to the old pattern). After a lapse: self-compassion prompt (JOY-08), a quick 'what got in the way?' tag, and a return plan with the minimum version; after long gaps: fresh-start reset (JOY-10) and possibly re-scoping the goal.
why: The relapse-prevention model distinguishes lapses from relapse and describes how an all-or-nothing reaction to a slip (abstinence-violation effect) can turn a lapse into relapse (Marlatt 1984); the exercise megastudy's top intervention rewarded returning after a missed workout (Milkman 2021).

sources.title: Relapse prevention: introduction and overview of the model
Megastudies improve the impact of applied behavioural science

safety_or_stop_rule: No shaming copy anywhere ('You failed', red X's).
notes: Marlatt's model comes from addictive behaviors; used here only as a conceptual framing.

name_en: Test nudges on herself; expect most to fade
what: Treat every nudge (reminder style, bundle, reward) as an experiment: run it for ~2–4 weeks, compare her logged behavior vs before, keep what works for her, drop the rest. Prioritize 'return after miss' micro-rewards.
why: In a 61,293-person megastudy of 54 four-week programmes, 45% increased weekly gym visits by 9–27%, the best offered micro-rewards for returning after a missed workout, only 8% had significant effects after the programme ended, and expert forecasts failed to predict winners (Milkman 2021).

sources.title: Megastudies improve the impact of applied behavioural science

safety_or_stop_rule: n-of-1 comparisons are noisy — don't over-interpret one week.
notes: Population: US fitness-chain members.

name_en: She is the author of the plan
what: The app suggests, explains why (rationale), and offers choices; she can edit, snooze or decline anything without penalty. Use non-controlling language ('you could', 'want to…?') rather than 'you must'. Support competence (achievable steps, informational feedback) and relatedness (optional connection features).
why: SDT-informed health interventions produced small-to-medium changes in health behavior, and increases in need support and autonomous motivation were associated with behavior change (Ntoumanis 2021, 73 studies); the METUX model applies basic psychological needs to technology design (Peters 2018).

sources.title: A meta-analysis of self-determination theory-informed intervention studies in the health domain: effects on motivation, health behavior, physical, and psychological health
Designing for Motivation, Engagement and Wellbeing in Digital Experience

safety_or_stop_rule: If she ignores most suggestions for 2+ weeks, the app asks what to change instead of escalating nudges.

what: Ban: confirmshaming ('No, I don't care about my health'), fake urgency/countdowns, guilt notifications, hidden opt-outs, nagging, forced continuity. Every nudge must be transparent and easy to turn off.
why: Dark patterns are interface choices that coerce, steer or deceive users into unintended decisions; a large-scale study found 1,818 instances across 15 types on ~11K shopping sites (Mathur 2019).

sources.title: Dark Patterns at Scale

safety_or_stop_rule: Any feature that works by pressure rather than her goals is removed.
notes: Mathur studied shopping sites; applying the taxonomy to a personal habit app is by analogy.
